According to data from the Crime Survey for England and Wales, around 2.1 million adults experienced domestic abuse in the year to March 2023; the majority of victims are women. Domestic abuse includes physical violence, controlling behaviour, economic abuse, coercive control and psychological harm. It predominantly occurs within intimate partner and family relationships.

Feminist sociologists argue that domestic violence is not an individual or pathological problem but a structural one rooted in patriarchy. The family, as an institution, concentrates male authority over women and children in a private space that is difficult for the state to monitor or regulate. Ann Oakley and other feminist sociologists argue that domestic violence is a manifestation of patriarchal power relations, not a failure of the family as an ideal but evidence that the family as it is currently structured systematically disadvantages women. This is the sharpest feminist challenge to the functionalist view that the family benefits all its members equally.

Functionalists respond to these criticisms by arguing that critics focus on the dysfunctions of family life while undervaluing its genuine benefits. Murdock and Parsons maintained that the family performs necessary functions — particularly primary socialisation and personality stabilisation — that no other institution performs as effectively. While dysfunctional families clearly exist, functionalists argue these represent failures of the institution rather than evidence against the institution itself. The New Right (Murray) shares the functionalist endorsement of the nuclear family but attributes its problems to family diversity — particularly lone parent families — rather than to any inherent flaw in the family as a structure.

Key Fact

Feminist sociologists argue that domestic violence is a structural consequence of patriarchy within the family, not an individual aberration. Functionalists argue that dysfunctional families are failures of the institution, not evidence against it — the family still performs irreplaceable primary socialisation. The two perspectives fundamentally disagree about whether the family as an institution is the problem or the solution.

lesson_title: Divorce: Causes, Consequences and Theoretical Perspectives
content_html:
Divorce in Britain Since 1945

Divorce is the legal ending of a marriage. The pattern of divorce in Britain since 1945 is one of dramatic and sustained increase, followed by a plateau and some decline in more recent years. In the decade after the Second World War, divorce was relatively rare — around 25,000 divorces per year in England and Wales. By the mid-1990s this had risen to around 175,000 per year. Since then the rate has declined somewhat, partly because marriage itself has become less common: more couples cohabit rather than marry, and fewer marriages can therefore end in divorce. Understanding the causes and consequences of this change is a central requirement of the families topic.

Legal Changes: The Divorce Reform Act 1969 and the 2022 No-Fault Reform

One of the most significant causes of the rising divorce rate was legal change. The Divorce Reform Act 1969, which came into force in 1971, fundamentally changed the legal basis of divorce in England and Wales. Before 1969, divorce required proof of a matrimonial “offence” such as adultery or cruelty. The 1969 Act replaced this with a single ground: irretrievable breakdown of marriage. This made divorce substantially easier and cheaper to obtain, and the divorce rate almost doubled in the years immediately after the Act came into force.

A further significant reform occurred in 2022 in England and Wales. The Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 (which came into force in April 2022) introduced no-fault divorce. Previously, even under the 1969 Act, one partner usually had to cite fault (such as adultery or unreasonable behaviour) to obtain a prompt divorce. The 2022 reform removed the need to attribute blame, making the process less adversarial. Sociologists note this reform may reduce the financial and psychological costs of divorce and could contribute to further changes in divorce statistics in the coming years.

Changing Social Attitudes and Secularisation

Legal change does not occur in a social vacuum. The 1969 Act reflected — and further accelerated — a broader shift in social attitudes towards divorce. As Britain became an increasingly secularised society, the religious stigma attached to divorce diminished. The Church of England and the Roman Catholic Church had traditionally taught that marriage was a lifelong sacrament and that divorce was morally wrong. As church attendance fell across the twentieth century and religious authority over personal life weakened, divorce became more socially acceptable. By the end of the twentieth century, divorce carried little social stigma in most communities.

More broadly, changing social values contributed to higher divorce rates. The growing expectation that marriage should provide personal fulfilment, romantic love and emotional intimacy — rather than simply economic partnership or social respectability — raised the bar for what constituted a “good enough” marriage. When marriages fell below this standard, individuals became more likely to seek divorce rather than continue in an unhappy relationship.

Key Fact

Four main reasons explain the rise in divorce since 1945: (1) legal change — the Divorce Reform Act 1969 introduced irretrievable breakdown as grounds for divorce; (2) the 2022 no-fault divorce reform reduced adversarial blame; (3) secularisation — declining religious stigma against divorce; (4) changing social attitudes and the changing status of women.

The Changing Status of Women

A particularly important cause of rising divorce rates is the changing status of women in society. Women’s increasing participation in paid employment since the Second World War gave many women greater economic independence. This reduced the financial dependence on a male partner that had previously made divorce an unviable option for many women. Research consistently shows that the majority of divorce petitions in England and Wales are filed by women — suggesting that women are more likely to seek to end unsatisfactory marriages when they have the economic means to do so.

The changing status of women is also linked to changing expectations: women’s greater social and political equality has raised their expectations of what a marriage should provide. The continued unequal distribution of domestic labour — Oakley’s double shift — means that many women experience marriage as disproportionately burdensome, and rising aspirations make this burden less acceptable over time.

Consequences of Divorce for Family Members

The consequences of divorce affect all members of the family. For partners, divorce can bring relief from an unhappy relationship but also significant emotional, financial and practical difficulties. Women tend to experience greater financial hardship after divorce, since they are more likely to have reduced their participation in paid employment during the marriage. Men tend to experience greater social isolation after divorce, since they are less likely to have primary care of children and may have weaker social networks outside the family.

For children, sociological research presents a complex picture. Some research suggests that parental conflict — not divorce itself — is the key factor in children’s outcomes. Divorce may in some cases be better for children than continuing in a highly conflicted marriage. Other research highlights the economic and social disadvantages associated with growing up in a lone parent household, including lower educational achievement and poorer health outcomes. Sociologists caution against treating all divorces as equally harmful, since outcomes vary significantly with income, quality of post-divorce parenting arrangements and the degree of continued conflict between former partners.

For the extended family, divorce disrupts grandparent–grandchild relationships and wider kinship networks. Grandparents on the non-resident parent’s side may lose contact with grandchildren entirely. The rise of divorce has also contributed significantly to the growth of lone parent families in the UK, since many divorces involve dependent children.

Serial monogamy describes the practice of having a succession of monogamous relationships or marriages — one at a time. As divorce has become more socially acceptable, more people go on to form new partnerships and remarry after divorce. Some functionalists interpret this as evidence that marriage as an institution remains highly valued: people seek it again after it breaks down rather than abandoning the institution entirely. Sociologists describe the growing prevalence of serial monogamy as reflecting the individualisation of relationship choice in contemporary society.

An empty shell marriage, by contrast, is a marriage that persists legally but in which the couple have effectively separated emotionally. Empty shell marriages may persist for financial reasons (such as maintaining a joint mortgage), social reasons (religious objection to divorce) or for the perceived benefit of children. This concept is important because it shows that official divorce statistics undercount the real number of relationships that have broken down.

Functionalist view: Parsons argued that the family adapts to meet social needs. Rising divorce rates may reflect rising expectations of what marriage should provide rather than signalling a crisis of the family. High remarriage rates support this: marriage as an institution remains valued, even if individual marriages fail.

Feminist view: Most divorce petitions are filed by women, supporting the feminist argument that marriage has historically placed greater burdens on women. Rising divorce rates reflect women’s growing economic independence and their capacity to leave unsatisfactory relationships. From this perspective, rising divorce is not a symptom of social breakdown but of women’s liberation from patriarchal constraints.

Marxist view: Marxists argue the causes of marital breakdown are often rooted in the economic conditions of capitalism — poverty, financial stress, the alienation of work and housing insecurity all increase pressure on family relationships. Zaretsky would see rising divorce as partly a consequence of the pressures capitalism places on workers and their families.

New Right view: Murray’s New Right perspective is critical of rising divorce rates, arguing that the growth of lone parent families resulting from divorce contributes to a dependency culture and the development of an underclass. Children raised without two parents are argued by the New Right to be educationally and socially disadvantaged. This view is challenged by feminist sociologists, who argue it pathologises lone parent families without addressing the structural causes of their difficulties.

Key Fact

The main consequences of divorce include: financial hardship (particularly for women); social isolation (particularly for men); varied impacts on children’s wellbeing; disruption of extended family relationships; and a significant increase in lone parent families. Serial monogamy and empty shell marriages show the complex reality behind divorce statistics.

lesson_title: Sociological Theories of the Role of Education
content_html:
What Is Education For?

Sociologists study education not simply as a place where skills are taught, but as a social institution that shapes values, reproduces inequality and connects individuals to wider society. Different sociological perspectives give very different answers to the question of what education is for — and whose interests it serves. The debate between consensus and conflict perspectives on education is one of the central disputes in GCSE Sociology.

Key Fact

The functionalist perspective argues education performs key functions for society: transmitting shared norms and values, creating social cohesion, teaching specialist skills, and allocating individuals to roles on meritocratic principles.

Durkheim: Transmission of Norms and Values

The French sociologist Émile Durkheim argued that education is the primary institution through which society transmits its norms and values to the next generation. Without this transmission, social solidarity — the shared sense of belonging that holds society together — would break down. Durkheim identified two main functions. First, education creates social solidarity: by teaching a shared history, language and culture, schools turn individual children into citizens who feel they belong to the same community. Second, education teaches specialist skills that the economy needs — mathematics, literacy, technical knowledge — enabling individuals to contribute to the division of labour in an industrialised society.

Parsons: Meritocracy and Achieved Status

Talcott Parsons extended Durkheim’s analysis. Parsons argued that schools act as a “bridge” between the family and wider society. In the family, a child is judged on particularistic standards — rules specific to that child. In wider society, however, people are judged on universalistic standards: the same rules apply to everyone, regardless of background. Parsons argued that schools prepare children for this shift by operating on meritocratic principles. Students who work hard earn high grades and access high-status jobs; those who do not earn lesser outcomes. The result is achieved status: social position reflects individual effort, not family background.

A meritocracy does not mean equal outcomes. It means that unequal outcomes are fair because they reflect effort and talent rather than background. Parsons’s point is that the inequality produced by a meritocracy is legitimate — it is earned. Critics from Marxist and feminist perspectives argue that schools do not in practice operate meritocratically, so the inequality they produce is not legitimate.

The Marxist Critique: Bowles and Gintis and the Correspondence Principle

Marxist sociologists challenge the functionalist view directly. Bowles and Gintis (Schooling in Capitalist America, 1976) argued that education does not serve society as a whole but primarily serves the bourgeoisie. Their correspondence principle holds that the organisation of schooling mirrors the organisation of the capitalist workplace. In schools, pupils obey teachers, follow rules and accept hierarchies — just as workers must obey managers. The hidden curriculum — the implicit lessons about conformity, hierarchy and obedience — prepares working-class pupils for lives of routine employment rather than critical citizenship.

For Bowles and Gintis, the appearance of meritocracy is a form of ideology: it convinces working-class pupils that their lower position results from their own lack of ability or effort, rather than from structural disadvantage. This serves the interests of capitalism by preventing challenge to the existing class order.

Key Fact

The hidden curriculum refers to the implicit lessons schools transmit alongside formal subjects: obedience to authority, punctuality, acceptance of hierarchy, gender-appropriate behaviour. Bowles and Gintis argued it mirrors the requirements of the capitalist workplace, preparing pupils for their class position. It is distinct from the formal curriculum (the timetabled subjects), which is the most common misconception in exam answers.

The Feminist Critique: Becky Francis and Patriarchal Schools

Feminist sociologists argue that the functionalist account ignores patriarchy. Becky Francis, in her research on gender and achievement, argued that schools remain patriarchal institutions: they reproduce gender inequality through classroom interaction, subject choice and teacher expectations. Francis identified two contrasting forms of gendered pupil behaviour — “laddish” behaviour among boys (disruptive, anti-academic, performed for peer status) and “under-the-radar rebellion” among girls (compliant in class but resistant in more subtle ways). Francis argued that teachers respond differently to each: boys’ disruption is often tolerated or treated as natural, while girls’ quieter resistance is less visible to teachers. These differential responses reinforce gendered identities and channel girls and boys into different educational pathways.

Functionalist: Education transmits shared norms and values, creates social solidarity, teaches specialist skills and allocates individuals to roles meritocratically. Durkheim (social cohesion and specialist skills) and Parsons (meritocracy and achieved status).

Marxist: Education reproduces class inequality through the correspondence principle and the hidden curriculum. Bowles and Gintis argue the appearance of meritocracy legitimises an unequal system, disguising class advantage as individual achievement.

Feminist: Education reproduces gender inequality. Becky Francis argues schools are patriarchal institutions that channel girls and boys into different roles through differential teacher responses and gendered expectations, reinforcing occupational segregation.

Interactionist: Rather than focusing on macro-level functions, interactionists examine how teacher labels, expectations and pupil interactions shape individual outcomes in classrooms. The self-fulfilling prophecy shows that teachers’ perceptions of pupils directly affect their achievements — a micro-level process that macro perspectives tend to overlook.

lesson_title: Processes Inside Schools
content_html:
What Happens Inside Schools?

Sociologists who focus on macro-level structures — class, capitalism, patriarchy — risk overlooking the daily processes within schools that shape individual outcomes. Interactionist sociologists argue that what happens in classrooms and corridors — how teachers perceive and label pupils, how pupils are grouped, how peer cultures develop — has a profound effect on achievement that cannot be explained solely by external factors such as class or home background.

Key Fact

Processes within schools affecting achievement include: streaming, setting, labelling, the self-fulfilling prophecy and the development of anti-school subcultures.

The Hidden Curriculum Revisited

Before examining labelling, it is important to be precise about the hidden curriculum. The hidden curriculum is not what appears on the timetable — that is the formal curriculum. The hidden curriculum refers to the implicit lessons schools transmit through their everyday routines and organisation: pupils learn to queue, sit in silence, accept the authority of the teacher, observe punctuality and behave in gender-appropriate ways. Bowles and Gintis (1976) linked the hidden curriculum directly to the correspondence principle: these lessons prepare working-class pupils for factory discipline and routine employment rather than critical independent thinking. In sport, boys and girls are often directed into different activities, reinforcing gendered norms of physical behaviour alongside academic learning.

Hargreaves: Labelling Deviant Pupils

David Hargreaves’s study Deviance in Classrooms (1975) examined how teachers label pupils as “deviant” within school settings. Hargreaves found that teachers rapidly formed assessments of pupils based on limited early interactions — assessments that then became stable and resistant to change. Pupils labelled as deviant or difficult tended to be placed in lower streams, received less academic encouragement and were disproportionately subject to formal discipline. Hargreaves argued that this labelling process was self-reinforcing: once a pupil was categorised as a “troublemaker”, subsequent behaviour — even relatively minor incidents — was interpreted through that lens. Hargreaves’s research is notable because it specifically focused on the school as the site of label formation, rather than locating the source of deviant identity in the pupil’s home background.

Becker and Master Status

Hargreaves’s findings connect to Howard Becker’s broader interactionist work on labelling. Becker (Outsiders, 1963) introduced the concept of master status: a label that overrides all other aspects of a person’s identity. In the school context, once a pupil is labelled as “a problem”, that label can become their master status, colouring every interaction they have with teachers. A pupil whose master status is “troublemaker” may find that even cooperative or positive behaviour is interpreted with suspicion. The self-fulfilling prophecy then follows: the pupil internalises the label and acts in ways that confirm it, transforming a teacher’s initial (possibly inaccurate) judgement into a social reality.

Stephen Ball’s study Beachside Comprehensive (1981) investigated the introduction and effects of banding in a secondary school. Ball found that the band a pupil was placed in at the start of secondary school significantly shaped their educational trajectory regardless of actual ability. Pupils in lower bands received a less academic curriculum, had lower teacher expectations placed on them, and developed more negative attitudes towards school. Ball demonstrated that banding was not a neutral administrative process — it was laden with social consequences, particularly for working-class pupils who were disproportionately placed in lower bands. The act of grouping by ability thus became a mechanism of class reproduction.

Paul Willis’s 1977 ethnographic study Learning to Labour followed twelve working-class boys (whom Willis called “the lads”) in a West Midlands comprehensive school. Willis found that “the lads” developed a counter-school culture: a system of values that actively opposed the school’s emphasis on academic work, obedience and qualifications. The lads valued masculine physical toughness, resistance to authority and the anticipation of manual labour, seeing conformist peers (“ear’oles”) as passive and weak.

Willis’s study is significant in several ways. First, it challenged Bowles and Gintis by showing that working-class pupils actively resist rather than passively absorb the hidden curriculum. Second, it revealed the paradox that this resistance — experienced by the lads as freedom — ultimately prepared them for working-class factory jobs just as effectively as conformity would have. Third, Willis drew on interactionist ideas about peer culture while grounding the analysis in a Marxist concern with class reproduction.

Key Fact

Labelling comes first: a teacher attaches a label (“troublemaker”, “high achiever”) to a pupil. The self-fulfilling prophecy describes what happens next: the pupil internalises the label and begins to act in ways that confirm it. Hargreaves showed that this process is particularly powerful in schools, where early labels quickly become stable and resistant to revision.

lesson_title: Patterns of Educational Achievement
content_html:
Reading the Data: What Do Achievement Patterns Show?

Before sociologists can explain educational inequality, they must first describe it accurately. This lesson focuses on patterns of educational achievement — what the data shows — rather than the causes, which are examined in the next lesson. The GCSE Sociology specification explicitly requires you to read and interpret attainment data: identifying a pattern from a table or chart, describing a trend over time, and noting which groups perform above or below the national average.

Key Fact

The three main dimensions of educational achievement studied at GCSE Sociology are social class, gender and ethnicity. For each, sociologists document consistent statistical patterns over time using official sources such as Department for Education data, the National Pupil Database and ONS statistics.

Patterns of Achievement by Social Class

Social class is the most consistent predictor of educational achievement in the UK. Pupils from higher social classes, on average, achieve higher GCSE grades and are significantly more likely to progress to sixth form and university than pupils from lower social classes. The most widely used measure of class-based attainment is eligibility for free school meals (FSM): consistently, pupils eligible for FSM achieve lower average grades at GCSE than their non-FSM peers. This gap has been documented across every year of available data and in every region of England and Wales.

To describe a class achievement pattern accurately, sociologists use statements such as: “In the most recent data, pupils not eligible for free school meals achieved a higher percentage of grade 5 and above in English and Maths than FSM-eligible pupils.” Notice this is a descriptive statement of pattern — it does not explain why this gap exists, which is the task of sociological theory.

When asked to interpret a table or chart in your exam, follow this two-step approach. First, identify the overall pattern: which group performs highest, which performs lowest? Is there a consistent gap between groups? Second, describe a trend over time: has the gap between groups widened, narrowed or stayed the same? Use specific figures from the data where given — for example, “Group A achieved 72%, compared with 48% for Group B, a gap of 24 percentage points.” Avoid vague language such as “Group A did better” without any supporting evidence from the data.

Patterns of Achievement by Gender

Until the late 1980s, boys outperformed girls in public examinations in the UK. Since the 1990s, this pattern has reversed: girls now consistently outperform boys at GCSE and A level on most measures. This reversal is one of the most significant shifts in UK educational patterns in recent decades. At GCSE, girls tend to achieve higher grades than boys in English, modern foreign languages and humanities; boys have historically performed better in some mathematics and science assessments, though this gap has narrowed significantly.

The gender gap at GCSE is not uniform across all subjects or all social classes. Some research suggests that the gap is largest among working-class pupils: working-class girls outperform working-class boys by a wider margin than the equivalent gap at middle-class level. This interaction between gender and class is important: it suggests that gender and class do not operate independently but intersect to shape attainment.

Patterns of Achievement by Ethnicity

UK educational data shows significant variation in achievement between different ethnic groups. Some groups perform consistently above the national average: pupils with Chinese and Indian heritage achieve among the highest average GCSE grades of any ethnic group. Other groups perform consistently below the national average: Black Caribbean boys and White British working-class boys are among the groups with the lowest average achievement. It is important to note two things when describing ethnic attainment patterns. First, there is substantial variation within ethnic groups — social class often mediates ethnic attainment significantly. Second, these are average patterns across large groups; individual pupils from any background may perform far above or below their group average.

Overall attainment at GCSE has risen since the introduction of the exam in 1988. However, the gaps between groups have proven persistent. The class gap has not closed significantly despite decades of educational policy: FSM pupils remain substantially behind their non-FSM peers. The gender gap in favour of girls has widened slightly since the 1990s. Ethnic attainment gaps have changed in a more complex way: some minority ethnic groups have seen rapid improvement (Indian, Chinese), while others have seen slower progress (Black Caribbean boys, White working-class boys). Describing these trends — not just the current snapshot — is what examiners reward at the higher mark bands.

Key Fact

Describing a pattern means identifying who performs above or below others at one point in time. Describing a trend means identifying whether the gap has changed over time. Both require sociological vocabulary: “attainment gap”, “free school meals eligibility”, “national average”, “overrepresented in lower attainment bands”. Vague descriptions (“poorer kids do worse”) earn minimal marks.

lesson_title: Factors Affecting Achievement: Class, Ethnicity and Gender
content_html:
Why Do Some Groups Achieve More Than Others?

The previous lesson described the patterns: working-class pupils perform below average, girls outperform boys since the 1990s, and ethnic groups show varied attainment. This lesson asks why. Sociologists organise explanations at two levels: factors outside school (home background, material resources, cultural attitudes) and factors inside school (labelling, streaming, curriculum content). No single perspective has the complete answer — competing explanations offer different mechanisms.

Key Fact

Outside-school factors include material deprivation and cultural capital. Inside-school factors include labelling, streaming, the ethnocentric curriculum, and catchment area effects linked to school type.

Social Class: Material and Cultural Factors

Material deprivation describes the economic disadvantages working-class pupils face: overcrowded housing with no quiet study space, inability to afford uniform or equipment, needing part-time jobs that reduce study time, and parents unable to pay for private tuition. These material conditions constrain performance regardless of ability or effort.

The concept of cultural capital was developed by Pierre Bourdieu. Bourdieu argued that middle-class families possess cultural capital — familiarity with the language, values and behaviours that schools reward. Middle-class children enter school already knowing how to address teachers, how to present written work and which cultural references carry currency. Working-class children often lack this, putting them at a systematic disadvantage even when equally able. The concept of cultural deprivation takes a related but different approach: it argues that some working-class family cultures transmit values that are misaligned with school expectations, such as short-term thinking over long-term academic investment. Critics argue this explanation “blames the victim” rather than addressing structural disadvantage.

Halsey: Class Barriers and Origins and Destinations

A.H. Halsey’s study Origins and Destinations (with Heath and Ridge, 1980) investigated the relationship between social class and educational achievement in Britain. Halsey found that despite the expansion of state education and the introduction of comprehensive schooling, class remained a powerful barrier to educational opportunity. Even when pupils of similar measured ability were compared, those from working-class backgrounds were significantly less likely to gain high-level qualifications or attend university. Halsey’s research is a direct challenge to the functionalist meritocracy claim: it demonstrates that achieved status in education reflects social background as much as individual talent.

Ball: Parental Choice, Catchment Areas and Marketisation

Stephen Ball’s research on marketisation and parental choice examined how league tables, Ofsted inspections and open enrolment reshaped inequality. Ball argued that middle-class families with cultural capital can navigate the system — reading league tables, visiting multiple schools and moving into desirable catchment areas. Working-class parents care equally about their children’s education but lack the same information and resources to act on their preferences. Counter-school cultures (Willis, 1977) also contribute: working-class boys who develop anti-school peer cultures limit their own qualifications, reproducing their class position through apparent free choice rather than coercion.

Explanations for ethnic attainment gaps divide into two broad camps. The cultural deprivation thesis argues that some minority ethnic families transmit cultural values misaligned with school expectations, such as different language practices or lower emphasis on formal academic qualifications. Critics regard this as “victim-blaming” and prefer structural explanations located in the school itself.

The ethnocentric curriculum describes a school curriculum that predominantly reflects White European culture and knowledge, potentially alienating minority ethnic pupils whose heritage and experience is not represented. Institutional racism refers to discrimination embedded in school policies and practices rather than in individual teacher attitudes — for example, disproportionate exclusion of Black Caribbean boys, or lower teacher expectations. The Macpherson Report (1999), following the Stephen Lawrence Inquiry, introduced institutional racism into mainstream British public debate and prompted reviews of school practices.

Feminist sociologists explain girls’ improved performance since the 1990s through changes in female aspirations, growth in service-sector employment for women, and curriculum reforms that moved away from male-dominated content. Girls have benefited from a broader expectation that academic qualifications lead to careers, rather than preparation for domestic roles.

The feminisation of schools refers to the claim that schools have become dominated by female teachers, coursework-based assessment and cooperative learning styles that suit girls more than boys, whose socialised learning behaviour differs. This remains a contested explanation among sociologists — some argue it pathologises boys rather than addressing wider structural inequality.

The crisis of masculinity describes the impact of de-industrialisation on working-class boys: as traditional male manual industries such as steel, coal and manufacturing declined from the 1980s onwards, some working-class boys came to see academic success as incompatible with masculine identity. With no clear vocational destination on the horizon, academic effort became associated with femininity and passivity. This explanation connects to Willis’s (1977) observation that “the lads” valued manual labour above academic work, anticipating futures in the factory rather than the classroom.

Key Fact

Material deprivation = lack of financial resources (no study space, no equipment, needing a part-time job). Cultural capital = lack of the middle-class knowledge and behaviours schools reward (unfamiliarity with teacher language, school conventions). Cultural deprivation = lack of the values and attitudes education systems expect. All three are associated with working-class underachievement but operate through different mechanisms — a pupil may experience one without the others.

lesson_title: Types of School and Educational Provision
content_html:
Why Does School Type Matter?

The UK has a diverse education system. Different types of school reflect different political priorities — about selection, competition, the role of the market, and who education is for. Sociologists from different perspectives disagree about whether this diversity is a strength or a source of inequality. Understanding the structural variety of school types is a distinct requirement in GCSE Sociology because the type of school a pupil attends shapes the opportunities available to them.

Key Fact

The main types of school in the UK are: comprehensive schools, grammar schools, academies, free schools, private (independent) schools and faith schools.

Primary and Secondary Education

State education in England and Wales is divided into primary schools (ages 5–11) and secondary schools (ages 11–16 or 18). The vast majority of children attend state schools funded by central government. Compulsory state education was introduced in the nineteenth century and gradually extended; all children in England must be in some form of education or training until the age of 18.

Comprehensive, Grammar and Selective Schools

Following the Education Act 1944, England adopted the tripartite system of grammar, technical and secondary modern schools, with pupils allocated by the eleven-plus examination. From the 1960s onwards, most local authorities replaced this with comprehensive schools that accept pupils of all abilities. Comprehensive education was associated with the principle that selection by ability at age eleven disadvantaged working-class children.

Grammar schools survive in parts of England. Supporters argue they provide high-achieving pupils from all backgrounds with access to a rigorous academic education. Critics — including many sociologists — argue that grammar schools entrench class inequality because middle-class families can afford private tuition to prepare their children for the eleven-plus while working-class families typically cannot. Welsh secondary schools are almost entirely comprehensive, with grammar schools remaining largely an English phenomenon.

Academies and Free Schools

Academies are state-funded but operate outside local authority control, with greater freedom over curriculum, pay and admissions. Free schools were introduced as a related policy and can be set up by any group — parents, teachers, charities or faith organisations — required to be non-selective and non-fee-paying. The expansion of academies and free schools is linked to the marketisation of education. The market logic assumes that competition between schools for pupils drives up standards. Sociologist Stephen Ball argued that marketisation benefits middle-class families who have the cultural capital and social networks to navigate school choice, while working-class families are disadvantaged.

Private and Faith Schools

Private schools — also called independent or public schools — are funded by fees and private endowments rather than the state. Approximately 7% of pupils in England attend private schools. Sociologists note that this small minority produces a disproportionate share of senior politicians, judges, top civil servants and university entrants to highly selective institutions, raising questions about whether private schooling reinforces class inequality and limits social mobility.

Faith schools are state-funded schools with a religious character, provided by faith organisations in partnership with the government. They exist across England and Wales and include Church of England, Roman Catholic, Jewish, Muslim and other faith communities. Faith schools may select a proportion of their intake on the basis of religious practice. From a functionalist perspective, faith schools transmit shared cultural values within communities. Critics — particularly from feminist and secular perspectives — argue that some faith schools reinforce gender inequality through their curriculum and expectations, or disadvantage pupils from different religious backgrounds in selective admissions.

Functionalist: A diverse range of school types allows the education system to match individuals to the roles best suited to their abilities, supporting meritocratic role allocation. Grammar schools and academies are seen as providing academic pathways for talented pupils from any background.

Marxist: The existence of fee-paying private schools alongside state schools reflects and reinforces class inequality. The bourgeoisie purchases educational advantage for their children, ensuring that privileged social positions are passed on rather than earned on merit.

Feminist: Historically, many elite schools were single-sex institutions designed for boys. Feminists have highlighted how comprehensive co-education improved girls’ access to the full curriculum, but argue that gender inequalities persist through subject choices and teacher expectations even within mixed schools. Some faith schools may reinforce traditional gender roles through their ethos.

New Right: Supporters of marketisation argue that parental choice and school competition drive up standards for all. Free schools and academies are welcomed as breaking the monopoly of local authority control and giving parents greater agency in choosing their children’s education.

Ball’s research on school choice showed that middle-class parents use their cultural capital to navigate the competitive market: they read league tables, visit multiple schools, write effective appeals and move into desirable catchment areas to access high-performing schools. Working-class parents make equally genuine choices but lack the same information, social networks and mobility. Ball’s argument is that the language of “parental choice” disguises a process that systematically advantages already privileged families, concentrating advantage and reinforcing the class gap in educational outcomes.

Key Fact

Both academies and free schools are state-funded but operate outside local authority control. The key difference is origin: academies are typically converted from existing state schools, while free schools are newly created by parents, charities or other groups. Both reflect the marketisation of education — the application of market principles (competition, consumer choice, performance measurement) to schooling.

lesson_title: Researching Education
content_html:
Why Does Research Method Matter in Education?

All the sociological knowledge discussed in this unit — from Bowles and Gintis on the correspondence principle to Willis on counter-school cultures, from Hargreaves on deviant labelling to Ball on teacher expectations — rests on research conducted in and about schools. The choice of research method shapes what a sociologist can find out. Different methods provide different types of data, carry different practical difficulties, and raise different ethical issues — particularly when the research subjects are children. Research methods permeate the whole of GCSE Sociology: every topic must be studied not just as content, but as something that has been researched in particular ways.

Key Fact

Sociologists researching education use: observation (participant or non-participant), interviews (structured or unstructured), questionnaires and secondary data such as official statistics, league tables and Ofsted reports.

Observation in Schools

Participant observation involves the researcher joining the group being studied — sitting in classrooms, spending time in corridors and building relationships with pupils and teachers over an extended period. Willis’s Learning to Labour (1977) is the most celebrated example: Willis spent months observing twelve working-class boys at a West Midlands comprehensive, attending lessons and informal gatherings. The strength of this method is validity: by immersing himself in the lads’ world, Willis gained rich, in-depth insight into their values and daily lives that a questionnaire could not have produced.

Non-participant observation involves watching what happens in classrooms without joining the group. This is less likely to change participants’ behaviour, but generates less detailed insight into meanings and motivations. Ball’s Beachside Comprehensive research used observation alongside interviews to investigate how banding shaped teacher expectations and pupil trajectories. A key weakness of any observation in schools is the risk of researcher influence: the presence of an observer changes the dynamic between teachers and pupils, potentially undermining validity.

Interviews and Questionnaires in Education Research

Unstructured interviews — open-ended conversations guided by broad topics rather than fixed questions — are particularly effective for exploring sensitive subjects such as the experience of being labelled by a teacher, or attitudes to school among disengaged pupils. They produce rich qualitative data. Halsey’s Origins and Destinations research combined survey data with follow-up interviews, using triangulation to increase confidence in the conclusions.

Questionnaires allow large-scale data collection from many respondents quickly and at low cost. They generate quantitative data that can be compared across schools and over time, producing high reliability. However, questionnaires are less effective at exploring why pupils hold particular attitudes or behave in particular ways — the “why” questions that interviews address better.

Official Statistics and League Tables

Sociologists researching educational achievement frequently use official statistics: GCSE and A-level results published by the Department for Education, Ofsted inspection reports, and national league tables. These sources are large-scale, longitudinal and freely available, allowing identification of trends in achievement across social class, gender and ethnicity over time. However, official statistics must be treated with critical caution. They are socially constructed — they reflect decisions about what to measure and how. League tables measure exam results but not the value a school adds to pupils’ progress. A school serving a disadvantaged intake may appear low-achieving by league table standards but be more educationally effective than a school in a wealthy catchment area.

Gaining access to schools is a major practical challenge. Schools are hierarchical institutions with multiple levels of gatekeepers: the headteacher must agree to the research, then individual teachers must open their classrooms, and parents must give consent for their children to participate. Each level of gatekeeping can limit or skew the data. Headteachers may only allow observation of “good” lessons, meaning the data does not represent everyday school life.

Researcher influence is a specific issue in schools: the presence of an unknown adult in the classroom changes pupil and teacher behaviour. Teachers may perform more carefully; pupils may behave differently in front of an observer. This reduces validity. Time and cost are further practical constraints: qualitative studies such as Willis’s required months of fieldwork, making them expensive and difficult to replicate on a larger scale.

Informed consent is particularly complex when research subjects are children. Sociologists must obtain consent from both the child and their parent or guardian. This requirement can introduce class bias: requiring parental written consent may reduce the sample to pupils whose parents are engaged and able to respond. Children must also be told clearly what the research involves and that they can withdraw at any time without penalty.

Confidentiality means protecting participants’ identities. Willis called his school “Hammertown”; Ball used the pseudonym “Beachside”. Pupils who share sensitive information — about bullying, poverty, family difficulties or experiences of labelling — must be assured that their identities are protected. However, confidentiality must be balanced against the duty to report serious safeguarding concerns. A researcher who discovers evidence of abuse cannot remain silent — the ethical obligation to protect the child overrides confidentiality.

Harm to participants includes psychological distress: asking pupils to describe experiences of labelling, exclusion or racism may cause upset. Researchers should use sensitive interview techniques, provide debriefing and ensure pupils know they can stop at any point. These strategies for addressing ethical issues are not a checklist to recite — they must be reasoned about in the specific research context.

Key Fact

The three key ethical issues in sociological research are: informed consent (especially complex with child participants — parental consent also required), confidentiality (protecting participants’ identities — Willis and Ball both used pseudonyms for their schools and participants) and harm to participants (psychological distress from sensitive questions; balanced against safeguarding duties). Sociologists must describe specific strategies to address each, not just list them.

lesson_title: Sociological Theories of Stratification
content_html:
What Is Social Stratification?

Social stratification refers to the system by which society ranks categories of people in a hierarchy. In every known human society, some groups enjoy greater wealth, status and power than others. Sociologists disagree fundamentally about why this unequal ordering exists, whether it serves useful purposes, and whether it is just. This lesson examines the conflict versus consensus debate on stratification, comparing the functionalist, Marxist, Weberian and feminist positions.

Key Fact

The four main perspectives on stratification are: functionalist (stratification is a necessary and meritocratic system), Marxist (stratification serves ruling-class interests through exploitation), Weberian (stratification is three-dimensional: class, status and party) and feminist (stratification reflects patriarchal power relations as much as class or merit).

The Consensus View: Functionalism and Davis and Moore

Writing from a functionalist perspective, Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore (1945) argued that social stratification performs two essential tasks for society: effective role allocation and performance linked to rewards. Their argument runs as follows: societies contain positions that vary in their functional importance — a surgeon performs a role more critical to social survival than many others. The pool of talented individuals capable of filling such roles is limited, so society must motivate the most talented to undergo the necessary training by attaching high rewards — high pay, prestige and status — to functionally important roles.

The result, in Davis and Moore’s view, is a meritocracy — a society in which positions are filled on the basis of ability and effort, not birth. Stratification is therefore not only inevitable but socially necessary: unequal rewards are the mechanism by which societies ensure the right people end up doing the most important jobs. A key early critic was Melvin Tumin, who challenged whether “functional importance” can be measured objectively and argued that stratification may actually restrict the talent pool by creating barriers for talented individuals from lower-class backgrounds.

An open system is one in which social mobility is possible — individuals can move up or down the hierarchy through their own efforts. Contemporary societies such as the UK are described as relatively open. Davis and Moore’s model assumes an open, meritocratic system in which talent finds its reward.

A closed system is one in which social position is fixed at birth and movement is not permitted. The caste system, historically practised in parts of South Asia, is the clearest example. Critics of Davis and Moore note that the UK class system has significant closed elements: privately educated individuals are over-represented in the highest professions, suggesting ascribed status continues to shape outcomes independently of talent.

The Conflict View I: Marxist Theory of Stratification

Karl Marx offered a fundamentally different account. From a Marxist perspective, stratification is not a neutral meritocratic mechanism — it is a system that serves the interests of the bourgeoisie at the expense of the proletariat. Marx argued that in capitalist society there are essentially two classes: those who own the means of production and those who are compelled to sell their labour. The relationship between them is one of exploitation: the bourgeoisie extract surplus value from workers’ labour, paying less in wages than the value workers create.

Marx introduced the concept of false class consciousness to explain why the proletariat do not always challenge their position: the ruling class uses ruling class ideology to make exploitation appear natural and inevitable. From this view, Davis and Moore’s functionalist theory is itself a form of ruling-class ideology — it legitimises unequal rewards as though they were purely meritocratic. Marx also used the concept of socio-economic classifications, recognising that in practice class positions are more complex than a simple two-class model, though he retained the bourgeoisie–proletariat division as the fundamental driver of social change.

The Conflict View II: Weberian Theory of Stratification

Max Weber agreed with Marx that class inequality was a powerful force, but argued that stratification could not be reduced to economics alone. Weber proposed a three-dimensional model: stratification operates through class (economic position in the market), status (social prestige and honour) and party (organised power and political influence). These three dimensions are related but not identical — a person may have high economic class but low social status (a newly wealthy person excluded from established social circles), or high status but limited economic resources (a declining aristocracy).

Weber also developed the concept of social closure — the way in which high-status groups maintain their position by restricting entry. Professional bodies that control who can enter a high-status occupation are practising social closure, using credentials and networks to exclude rivals. Weber’s three-dimensional model is often seen as offering a more nuanced account of inequality than Marx’s two-class model, because it can explain forms of inequality — ethnic, religious, status-based — that are not reducible to ownership of the means of production.

Students sometimes treat stratification as purely about income. Weber’s three-dimensional model is a direct challenge to this. A person’s position in the stratification system depends on their market position (class), their social prestige (status) and their access to collective power (party). These can diverge significantly. An examiner-flagged error is to describe any high-income person as “high class” in Weber’s terms — Weber would require analysis of market position, status group membership and political influence separately. A Mastering-tier answer on a 12-mark Evaluate question will contrast the Marxist two-class economic model with the Weberian multidimensional framework.

The Conflict View III: Feminist Theory and Patriarchy

Feminist sociologists argue that both functionalist and Marxist accounts of stratification overlook the significance of gender as an independent dimension of inequality. Where Davis and Moore see reward levels as reflecting functional importance, and Marx sees them as reflecting class exploitation, feminist sociologists point out that neither adequately explains why women’s labour — both in the paid workforce and in domestic life — has historically been undervalued.

Sylvia Walby (1990) argued that patriarchy is an independent structural system that operates alongside class. Care work, nursing and teaching — predominantly female occupations — tend to be rewarded less highly than male-dominated professions requiring comparable training, not because they are less functionally important but because reward levels reflect gender power relations. Feminist sociologists also note that stratification systems have historically restricted women from access to education, professional training and political participation, regardless of their individual talent — a direct challenge to the meritocratic claims of Davis and Moore.

Key Fact

In a 12-mark Evaluate question on stratification, the highest marks come from presenting all four perspectives: functionalist (Davis and Moore — meritocratic necessity), Marxist (stratification serves ruling-class interests), Weberian (three-dimensional class–status–party model, social closure) and feminist (patriarchy as an independent system of stratification). Close with a supported judgement about which perspective offers the most convincing explanation.

lesson_title: Power and Authority: Weber's Three Types
content_html:
Power and Authority: Key Concepts

In sociology, power and authority are closely related but distinct concepts. Power refers to the capacity to get others to do what you want, regardless of whether they consent — this can include coercion, force or threat. Authority refers to power that is considered legitimate: people comply because they believe the person or institution exercising power has the right to do so. A police officer who physically restrains someone exercises power; a judge who imposes a sentence exercises authority because the sentence is backed by a legal framework that most people accept as legitimate.

Max Weber (1947) distinguished three distinct types of authority based on the different grounds on which people accept another’s right to exercise power over them. These three types — traditional, charismatic and rational-legal — are among the most important concepts in the sociology of power and are directly assessed in your exam.

Key Fact

Weber’s three types of legitimate authority are: traditional (based on custom and inherited status), charismatic (based on exceptional personal qualities) and rational-legal (based on formal rules and offices). Each has a different source of legitimacy and different implications for how power operates in society.

Weber’s Three Types of Authority

Traditional authority is the oldest form of legitimate power. It rests on the belief that certain customs, institutions and rulers have always existed and therefore have an established right to exercise authority. Obedience is owed to the person who holds a traditional office, not to any particular set of rules. The clearest UK example is the monarchy: the legitimacy of the Crown rests on hereditary succession and centuries of custom, not on any written mandate from the people or formal qualifications. The power of landlords over tenants in feudal society was similarly traditional.

Charismatic authority derives not from rules or tradition but from the personal qualities of the individual — their vision, magnetism, communication skills or perceived special destiny. Followers obey because they believe in the leader as a person, not because of the office they hold. Charismatic authority is inherently unstable because it depends on the continued belief of followers and cannot easily be passed on. When a charismatic leader dies or loses followers’ trust, their authority typically either disappears or is “routinised” into traditional or rational-legal form. A religious leader or a political leader who builds a movement through personal appeal provides a sociological illustration.

Rational-legal authority is the form Weber saw as characteristic of modern bureaucratic societies. Its legitimacy rests on the acceptance of formal rules, laws and procedures. People obey not because of custom or personal charisma but because they accept the legitimacy of the legal framework. Authority is attached to offices rather than individuals — an elected Member of Parliament or a judge exercises authority because of the office they hold under the constitutional framework, not because of who they personally are. Weber saw the growth of rational-legal authority as fundamental to modern capitalist societies.

Students frequently apply the wrong type to examples. Key tests: Is the authority based on rules and formal offices? → rational-legal. Is it based on custom and who you were born as? → traditional. Is it based purely on personality and personal devotion to the leader? → charismatic. Common errors: labelling a popularly elected Prime Minister as “charismatic” because they are popular — they hold rational-legal authority because their power rests on formal electoral rules, not personal devotion. Calling a hereditary peer “rational-legal” — they hold traditional authority because their position is inherited, not based on a formal qualification or election.

Formal and Informal Sources of Power

Weber’s three types of authority are all forms of formal power — power that operates through official channels. But power is also exercised informally. Informal power operates outside official structures. Economic power — an employer’s ability to dismiss or reward workers — is a form of informal power not necessarily embedded in law. Cultural prestige can shape behaviour without any formal authority. Within family relationships, patriarchal power can operate informally through gendered expectations and the division of domestic labour. Weber also identified social closure as a mechanism of informal power: professional bodies that control entry to high-status occupations restrict access to valued resources.

Agencies of Social Control

Power in society is exercised not just by individuals but through agencies of social control — institutions that monitor and regulate behaviour to maintain social order. Agencies of social control can be formal or informal. Formal agencies have official, legally defined powers: the police enforce criminal law; the courts administer justice; the prison system punishes offenders. Schools exercise formal authority over young people through attendance laws and disciplinary powers. Informal agencies exercise social control through norms, peer pressure and socialisation rather than legal compulsion: the family, peer groups and the media all shape behaviour by rewarding conformity and stigmatising deviance. The distinction between formal and informal agencies is important because much social control is achieved informally, without the direct exercise of legal power.

Functionalists tend to view legitimate authority — especially rational-legal authority — as a functional necessity for social order. The 2024 examiner report noted that stronger candidates understood that functionalists accept power differences exist but see them as “inevitable and necessary” for the smooth running of society. Authority structures serve the common good rather than any one group’s interests.

Marxists argue that in capitalist societies, authority structures ultimately serve the interests of the bourgeoisie. Ruling class ideology makes the state’s authority appear neutral and legitimate when in practice it protects the property rights and economic position of those who own the means of production. Weber’s rational-legal framework, from a Marxist perspective, obscures the class basis of state power.

Feminist sociologists argue that authority structures are patriarchal: historically, both traditional authority (inherited male power in monarchies and patriarchal families) and rational-legal authority (legal systems that long denied women voting rights and professional access) have operated to maintain male dominance. Walby’s identification of the state as one of the six structures of patriarchy is directly relevant here.

Key Fact

Weber’s three types of authority are frequently tested in 3-mark Identify and Describe and 4-mark Describe questions. Know the name, the source of legitimacy and at least one example of each. Do not call elected officials ‘charismatic’ — their authority is rational-legal because it derives from constitutional rules, not personal devotion.

lesson_title: Inequality in Contemporary UK: Class, Gender, Ethnicity
content_html:
Equality and Inequality in Contemporary UK

Sociologists use a wide range of evidence to map inequality in the UK. Social inequality refers to the unequal distribution of valued resources — income, wealth, health, education and social power — between different groups. The spec asks students to consider evidence of inequality across seven named domains and to understand how inequality is produced and sustained through processes such as discrimination, stereotyping, labelling and scapegoating.

Key Fact

The spec identifies seven key domains where inequality is documented in contemporary UK: income and wealth, education, crime, health, family, work and media representation. Inequality in each domain can be explained by structural factors (class, patriarchy, institutional racism) and by processes operating at the individual and institutional level.

Evidence of Inequality Across Seven Domains

Income and wealth: The distribution of income and wealth in the UK remains highly unequal. The highest-earning households earn many times more than those at the lowest end. ONS data consistently shows that the top fifth of households receive a disproportionate share of total household income. Wealth inequality is even more pronounced: ownership of property and assets is concentrated in relatively few hands.

Education: Children from professional and managerial backgrounds significantly outperform those from working-class backgrounds in national assessments. Private schooling reinforces class-based advantage. Gender gaps have shifted: girls now outperform boys at GCSE and A level in many subjects, but subject choice and occupational destination remain gendered. Some ethnic minority groups face additional barriers linked to cultural deprivation arguments, ethnocentric curriculum content and, in some cases, institutional racism.

Crime: Official statistics show that people from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and from some ethnic minority groups are over-represented in arrest, prosecution and imprisonment data. However, sociologists are careful to note that official crime statistics reflect policing and prosecution patterns as much as actual offending. The moral panic around certain groups — young Black men in relation to knife crime, for example — illustrates how media representations and labelling can amplify perceptions of criminality beyond what the evidence supports.

Health: There are significant and persistent health inequalities by social class in the UK. Life expectancy, infant mortality, mental health outcomes and chronic disease all follow a clear social gradient — the lower a person’s class position, the worse their average health outcomes. Gender and ethnicity intersect with class: women live longer on average but report higher rates of depression; some ethnic minority groups face higher rates of certain conditions partly linked to socioeconomic disadvantage.

Family: Family forms are distributed unequally across class and ethnicity. Lone-parent families are more likely to be in poverty, partly because they depend on a single income and face greater childcare costs. Working-class families are less likely to have access to material resources and social capital that ease family functioning. Research also documents a persistent gender inequality within many families: women continue to carry a disproportionate share of domestic labour and childcare (Oakley’s double shift).

Work: The gender pay gap persists across most sectors. Women are over-represented in part-time and lower-paid “feminised” occupations. The glass ceiling continues to restrict women’s access to senior roles. Some ethnic minority workers face hiring discrimination and are under-represented in higher management despite comparable qualifications.

Media representation: Media representations of different social groups can perpetuate stereotypes. Women are frequently represented in a limited range of roles — domestic, decorative or subordinate to men. Ethnic minority groups have historically been under-represented or negatively stereotyped in mainstream UK media. Working-class people may be represented through negative stereotypes (the “chav”, benefit fraud) that scapegoat them for structural problems. These representations can feed into labelling processes and reinforce prejudice.

Private schooling is one of the most visible mechanisms through which class inequality is reproduced. Around 7% of UK children attend private schools, yet their alumni are consistently over-represented in elite occupations — senior law, medicine, politics, finance and the media. The advantage is not solely academic: private schools provide access to social networks and cultural capital that public schools typically cannot. The informal network of contacts, shared school ties and mutual recognition among privately educated individuals is sometimes described as the “old boys’ network” — a form of social closure that operates to preserve elite advantage across generations.

Fiona Devine’s study Affluent Workers Revisited (1992) examined social class identity and inequality from a different angle. Revisiting the site of Goldthorpe and Lockwood’s 1960s Luton car-plant study, Devine interviewed manual workers and their partners. She found that claims of widespread embourgeoisement — the idea that affluent working-class people had absorbed middle-class values and abandoned class identity — were overstated. Workers retained a strong sense of class identity and resentment at extreme inequality, even as many aspired to consumer goods. Devine’s study is important for Eduqas/WJEC students because it challenges the idea that class inequality has diminished with rising living standards, and demonstrates that class identity and awareness of inequality persist even among relatively well-paid workers.

Gender Inequality: Walby on Patriarchy

Sylvia Walby (1990) argued that patriarchy is not simply a matter of individual discrimination but a structural system operating through six institutions simultaneously: paid work, household production, patriarchal culture, sexuality, male violence and the state. Each structure independently restricts women’s power. The gender pay gap, the double shift, media double standards on women’s behaviour, and under-representation in elected office are all, in Walby’s analysis, expressions of this multi-institutional system. Walby also identified a historical shift from private patriarchy (women controlled directly in the family home) to public patriarchy (women formally included in public life but collectively disadvantaged within it). Contemporary crisis of masculinity debates link changes in the labour market (loss of traditional male manufacturing jobs) to shifts in gender identity, suggesting that patriarchal structures are under pressure even as they persist.

Ethnicity Inequality: Racism and Institutional Racism

Ethnic inequality in the UK operates through both individual prejudice and institutional racism — the systematic disadvantage built into the practices and culture of organisations. The MacPherson Report (1999) applied this concept to the Metropolitan Police following the Stephen Lawrence inquiry. Employment studies using matched CVs have demonstrated that applicants with African or Asian-sounding names receive fewer interview invitations than identical applications with traditionally White British names, suggesting that direct discrimination remains a real factor alongside structural disadvantage.

Government and parliament have attempted to address inequality through legislation. The Equality Act 2010 consolidated earlier legislation (Equal Pay Act, Sex Discrimination Act, Race Relations Act) into a single framework, establishing nine protected characteristics including age, disability, gender reassignment, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Employers and service providers are legally prohibited from discriminating on these grounds. Sociologists evaluate the effectiveness of this legislation differently: functionalists may see it as evidence that the system is self-correcting toward meritocracy; Marxists argue that formal legal equality does not address structural economic inequality; feminists point to persistent gaps — especially the gender pay gap — as evidence that legislation alone is insufficient where patriarchal structures remain intact.

Key Fact

Devine’s 1992 restudy found that affluent manual workers retained strong class identities and resentment at extreme inequality, contradicting the embourgeoisement thesis. This shows that class inequality is experienced and felt by workers even when living standards rise — rising wages do not dissolve class identity or awareness of structural unfairness.

lesson_title: Inequality: Age, Disability, Sexuality and Religion
content_html:
Inequality Beyond Class and Gender

The GCSE Sociology specification recognises that inequality is not produced only by class or gender. Age, disability, sexuality and religion are each named as dimensions of social inequality that shape the life chances and power of different groups in the UK. Sociologists study these inequalities using the same tools applied to class and gender: evidence of disadvantage, analysis of the mechanisms that produce it, and perspectives that offer competing explanations. This lesson examines each in turn, giving particular attention to the medical and social models of disability — a binary the specification explicitly requires students to explain.

Key Fact

The specification requires students to distinguish two models of disability: the medical model (disability is the impairment in the individual) and the social model (disability is created by societal barriers). These models lead to fundamentally different conclusions about where the “problem” of disability lies and therefore who is responsible for addressing it.

Age Inequality and Ageism

Ageism is the term sociologists use to describe prejudice or discrimination based on age. Unlike some other protected characteristics, ageism affects people at both ends of the age spectrum — the young and the elderly — in different ways.

Youth inequality: Young people in the UK face specific disadvantages. They are over-represented in unemployment statistics and are less likely to own their own homes than previous generations at the same life stage. Young people below the age of 18 cannot vote and have limited political power. Media representations of young people frequently rely on negative stereotypes — the “feral youth”, the anti-social teenager — which can feed into scapegoating of young people for social problems such as crime and benefit dependency. These representations involve a form of labelling that can have real consequences for how young people are treated by police, employers and schools.

Elderly inequality: Older people face a different pattern of disadvantage. Workers over fifty may be passed over for promotion or made redundant in favour of younger employees, in a process of ageist discrimination that limits their earning power and economic security. Older people on fixed or state pensions are vulnerable to poverty, especially when the cost of living rises. Social isolation is more common among older people, limiting their participation in social life. Under-representation of older people in elected politics means their interests — in areas such as social care funding, pension provision and healthcare — may be under-prioritised relative to working-age adults. Functionalists might argue that different treatment of the elderly reflects the reduced functional contribution of those who have retired from active employment; conflict perspectives argue that ageism serves the interests of employers and the state by pushing older workers out of the labour market at reduced cost.

Disability Inequality: Medical and Social Models

Disability is one of the most debated areas of social inequality because sociologists disagree about what disability fundamentally is. The two dominant frameworks are the medical model of disability and the social model of disability.

Medical model: The medical model locates disability within the individual. A person who uses a wheelchair is “disabled” because their body cannot perform the function of walking. The solution, in this framework, is medical intervention — treatment, rehabilitation or prosthetics — to restore the individual as closely as possible to a “normal” state. The focus is on what is “wrong” with the person. Critics argue this model individualises a social problem, treating disabled people as passive patients who need to be “fixed” rather than as citizens who face structural barriers. Historically the medical model has been used to justify institutionalisation and has reinforced stigma by associating disability with deficit.

Social model: The social model, developed by disabled activists and sociologists from the 1970s onwards, locates disability in society rather than in the individual. A person who uses a wheelchair is “disabled” not by their inability to walk but by the absence of ramps, lifts and accessible buildings. The impairment (the physical condition) is distinguished from the disability (the disadvantage created by social barriers). In this framework, the solution is to remove social barriers — to build accessible environments, challenge discriminatory attitudes, and change employment practices. The social model aligns most closely with the sociological discipline because it treats disability as a form of social construction rather than a fixed biological category. Most sociologists prefer the social model because it is consistent with the broader sociological principle that inequality is produced by social arrangements, not by nature. For example: two people with the same hearing impairment may have very different experiences depending on whether their workplace provides British Sign Language interpreters, captioning technology and flexible communication policies. The impairment is the same; the disability (social exclusion, restricted employment) is variable because it depends on social provision.

In contemporary UK, disabled people face significant inequality in employment, income and social participation. The disability employment gap — the difference in employment rates between disabled and non-disabled people — remains substantial. Disabled people are, on average, paid less and are more likely to be in poverty. The Equality Act 2010 places duties on employers to make “reasonable adjustments” to remove barriers, but campaigners argue enforcement is weak and attitudinal barriers remain significant.

Sexuality Inequality: Homophobia and Heteronormativity

Homophobia refers to prejudice, discrimination and hostility directed at people on the grounds of their sexuality. LGBTQ+ individuals have faced, and in many contexts continue to face, significant inequality. In the UK, same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in England and Wales in 1967 (and later in Scotland and Northern Ireland). Civil partnerships were introduced in 2004, and same-sex marriage was legalised in England and Wales in 2013. These legal changes mark significant shifts in formal equality.

However, sociologists distinguish formal legal equality from lived experience. Heteronormativity — the cultural assumption that heterosexuality is the default — continues to operate through everyday interactions, institutional culture and media representation, even after legal equality has been achieved. Research consistently shows that LGBTQ+ individuals report higher rates of mental health difficulties, including depression and anxiety, linked to experiences of discrimination, bullying and social exclusion. Hate crimes on grounds of sexual orientation continue to be recorded by UK police. Employment discrimination, while illegal, remains reported in survey evidence.

Sociologists working in the interactionist tradition draw attention to how labelling and stigma operate around sexual orientation. Being labelled as “different” or “deviant” in educational and social settings can have lasting effects on mental health and social participation. Feminist sociologists link homophobia to patriarchal norms — gay men and lesbian women challenge traditional gender roles and the heterosexual family form that patriarchal culture treats as normal, meaning homophobia can be understood partly as a defence of patriarchal norms.

Religious Inequality: Islamophobia and Antisemitism

Religion and belief is a recognised dimension of inequality in the UK. The specification explicitly names Islamophobia and antisemitism as documented forms of religious inequality.
